questions.question: How do you identify classes from a problem statement in LLD?
questions.interviewer_intent: Check entity identification skill — the first step of any LLD
questions.direct_answer: Identify nouns in the problem statement — these become candidate classes. Filter to entities that have both data (attributes) and behavior (methods). Actors become interfaces or abstract classes.

items: Nouns → candidate classes: Vehicle, ParkingSpot, Ticket, Payment
Verbs → methods on classes: park(), calculateFee(), issueTicket()
Not everything needs its own class: simple value objects can be fields
Actors (users, systems): often interfaces or abstract classes
Value objects vs entities: ParkingSpot (entity) vs Price (value object)
Group related attributes together into a class

answer_sections.content: My technique for identifying classes: I underline all the nouns in the problem statement. For a parking lot: parking lot, floor, spot, vehicle, car, motorcycle, ticket, payment, display board. These are my candidate classes. Then I filter: does it have meaningful attributes AND behaviors? ParkingSpot has attributes (spotId, type, isOccupied) and behaviors (occupy(), free(), isAvailable()) — it's a class. 'Price' might just be a BigDecimal field, not its own class. Verbs tell me what methods belong to which class: 'issue a ticket' → Ticket has an issueTicket() or the ParkingLot has issueTicket() that creates a Ticket. I also identify abstract concepts: Vehicle is abstract because the concrete types are Car and Motorcycle.

speakable_v2.hook: Every LLD starts with one question: what are my classes? Here's the technique that makes it almost mechanical.

beats.text: Identifying classes is the first step in any LLD. The trick is to read the problem statement and underline every noun — those are your candidate classes.

items: Underline nouns: parking lot, floor, spot, vehicle, car, motorcycle, ticket, payment
Filter candidates: does it have both meaningful attributes AND behaviors?
Verbs become methods: 'issue a ticket' means Ticket.issue() or ParkingLot.issueTicket()
Actors (users, external systems) often become interfaces or abstract classes
Simple values like price may just be a field — not every noun needs its own class

beats.text: ParkingSpot has attributes (spotId, type, isOccupied) and behaviors (occupy(), free(), isAvailable()) — it earns its own class. 'Price' is often just a BigDecimal field on another class, not a class by itself.
candidates miss: identifying abstract concepts. Vehicle is abstract because the concrete types are Car and Motorcycle — make that explicit early or you'll redesign later.

speakable_v2.cap: Underline nouns, filter by attributes-plus-behaviors, then check for abstract concepts. That three-step scan will get you a solid class list in two minutes.

questions.question: What is the difference between an abstract class and an interface in LLD?
questions.interviewer_intent: Test OOP fundamentals applied to design choices
questions.direct_answer: Abstract class: partial implementation, for IS-A with shared code (Vehicle with common fields). Interface: contract only, for CAN-DO relationships (Payable, Parkable). Use interface for type hierarchy, abstract class for shared implementation.

answer_sections.content: In LLD, I use abstract class when there's a clear IS-A relationship with shared implementation. Vehicle is abstract because all vehicles share common attributes (licensePlate, size, color) and the subclasses (Car, Motorcycle) build on that. I use interfaces for capabilities or contracts that can apply to unrelated classes. Payable could apply to a Vehicle or a ParkingSubscription — they're not related by IS-A but both can be paid for. The rule: abstract class for shared code in a family of classes; interface for defining a contract that any class can implement. In modern Java, interfaces can have default methods, which blurs this a bit, but the design intent remains distinct.

follow_up_questions: Can a class extend an abstract class and implement interfaces simultaneously?
When would you change a class to an interface in a design?

speakable_v2.standard_example: Java class hierarchy for a parking lot system
speakable_v2.hook: Abstract class vs interface is one of the most common LLD follow-ups — and the answer isn't about Java syntax, it's about design intent.

groups.heading: Abstract Class
groups.text: A partial implementation meant to be extended. Use it when related classes share code. Vehicle is abstract because Car and Motorcycle both need licensePlate, color, and size fields.

groups.heading: Interface
groups.text: A contract that defines capabilities. Use it when unrelated classes need the same behavior. Payable could apply to a Vehicle or a ParkingSubscription — they're not related by IS-A, but both can be paid for.

beats.text: Use abstract class for shared code in a family. Use interface for defining a capability that any class can implement. When in doubt, start with an interface — it's easier to loosen later than to break inheritance hierarchies.
sharp edge: Java interfaces now support default methods, which blurs the line. But the design intent still matters — don't use default methods to smuggle shared state into an interface.

speakable_v2.cap: Abstract class = shared code for an IS-A family. Interface = a contract for a CAN-DO capability. Start with interface when you're unsure.

questions.question: How do you define the responsibilities of each class in an LLD?
questions.interviewer_intent: Test SRP application — each class should have one reason to change
questions.direct_answer: Apply SRP: each class should have one reason to change. ParkingSpot manages spot availability. FeeCalculator calculates fees. TicketGenerator creates tickets. Don't combine unrelated behaviors in one class.

answer_sections.content: I apply the Single Responsibility Principle: each class should have one primary reason to change. In a parking lot: ParkingSpot's job is tracking whether it's occupied and what type it is — nothing about pricing. FeeCalculator calculates fees based on time and vehicle type — nothing about spots. TicketGenerator creates and manages tickets. ParkingLot coordinates the overall flow: find a spot, issue a ticket, process exit. A sign of poor SRP is a 'God class' that knows about spots, fees, tickets, and display boards. When you ask 'why would this class change?' and get three different answers, it needs to be split. Each business rule change should ideally only require changing one class.

follow_up_questions: How does SRP relate to the concept of cohesion?
What happens to your design if you violate SRP?

speakable_v2.standard_example: Java class hierarchy for a parking lot system
speakable_v2.hook: The Single Responsibility Principle sounds obvious — until you're staring at a 500-line class that does everything.

beats.text: SRP says each class should have one primary reason to change. It's the most practical LLD principle because it directly shapes which classes you create and what goes in each.

groups.heading: ParkingSpot
groups.text: Tracks whether it's occupied and what type it is. Nothing about pricing.

groups.heading: FeeCalculator
groups.text: Calculates fees based on time and vehicle type. Nothing about spots.

groups.heading: TicketGenerator
groups.text: Creates and manages tickets. Knows entry time, spot, and vehicle.

groups.heading: ParkingLot
groups.text: Coordinates the overall flow: find a spot, issue a ticket, process exit. It delegates the details.

beats.text: production trap: the 'God class' — a ParkingLot that also calculates fees, generates tickets, and updates displays. Ask yourself: 'why would this class change?' If you get three different answers, it needs to be split.

speakable_v2.cap: Give each class one job. If you can describe a class's responsibility in one short sentence, you're on the right track.

questions.question: What are enums useful for in LLD and how do you use them?
questions.interviewer_intent: Check practical Java LLD skill — enums are heavily used in class design
questions.direct_answer: Enums represent fixed sets of constants with associated behavior. In LLD: VehicleType (CAR, MOTORCYCLE, TRUCK), SpotType (COMPACT, LARGE, HANDICAPPED), TicketStatus (ACTIVE, PAID, EXPIRED). Better than String constants.

answer_sections.content: Enums are extremely useful in LLD for representing a fixed set of states or types. Instead of using String constants or magic integers, enums give type safety and readability. In a parking lot: VehicleType enum with CAR, MOTORCYCLE, TRUCK — now the compiler catches if I accidentally pass 'BUS' which isn't a valid type. SpotType with COMPACT, LARGE, HANDICAPPED. TicketStatus with ACTIVE, PAID, EXPIRED. Java enums can also carry data and behavior — SpotType.COMPACT can have a size field. Using enums in switch statements is clean and the compiler warns if you miss a case. They also make persistence more explicit — store the enum name as a string in the database.

follow_up_questions: How do you store an enum value in a database with JPA?
Can Java enums have abstract methods?

speakable_v2.standard_example: Java class hierarchy for a parking lot system
speakable_v2.hook: Enums are small but powerful — and every LLD that has types or states should be using them.

beats.text: Enums represent a fixed set of constants. In LLD they replace error-prone String constants and magic integers — and the compiler enforces valid values for you.

items: VehicleType: CAR, MOTORCYCLE, TRUCK — type-safe vehicle classification
SpotType: COMPACT, LARGE, HANDICAPPED — each can carry a size field
TicketStatus: ACTIVE, PAID, EXPIRED — state machine for a ticket's lifecycle
PaymentMode: CASH, CARD, UPI — clean switch statements with compiler warnings if you miss a case

beats.text: SpotType.COMPACT can carry its own size field and a getSize() method. That's richer than a plain constant — it bundles the data and behavior that belong together.
non-obvious: Java enums can have abstract methods, meaning each constant can override the behavior differently. It's rarely needed in LLD interviews, but it shows depth if you mention it.

speakable_v2.cap: Reach for enums whenever you have a fixed set of types or states. They make your design safer, clearer, and easier to extend.

questions.question: How do you model a one-to-many relationship in LLD Java classes?
questions.interviewer_intent: Check understanding of composition and collection relationships
questions.direct_answer: Use a collection field: ParkingLot has List<ParkingFloor> floors. The 'one' side holds a collection of the 'many' side. Add methods to add, remove, and query from the collection.

answer_sections.content: One-to-many in Java classes is straightforward: the 'one' side holds a collection of the 'many'. ParkingLot has a List<ParkingFloor>. ParkingFloor has a Map<String, ParkingSpot> keyed by spot ID. The choice of collection type matters: List for ordered sequences, Set for unique items, Map for keyed lookup. I expose the relationship through methods rather than directly exposing the collection: addFloor(), getAvailableSpots(vehicleType), rather than getFloors() which exposes the internal list. This encapsulation lets me change the internal structure later — switch from List to Map for better spot lookup performance — without changing callers.

follow_up_questions: When would you use a Map instead of a List for a one-to-many relationship?
How do you handle bidirectional relationships in LLD?

speakable_v2.standard_example: Java class hierarchy for a parking lot system
speakable_v2.hook: One-to-many is the most common relationship in LLD — and Java collections are exactly how you express it.

beats.text: A one-to-many relationship means one object owns or contains multiple instances of another. In Java, the 'one' side holds a collection field pointing to the 'many' side.

ParkingLot has a List of ParkingFloor. Each ParkingFloor has a Map keyed by spotId to ParkingSpot. The Map is better than a List here because you'll look up a spot by ID far more often than you'll iterate in order.

items: List: use when order matters or you need index access
Set: use when uniqueness matters and order doesn't
Map: use when you need fast lookup by a key — spot ID, vehicle license plate

beats.text: gotcha: don't expose the internal collection directly via a getFloors() getter. Expose it through meaningful methods like addFloor() and findAvailableSpot(). This lets you change the internal data structure later without breaking callers.

speakable_v2.cap: The 'one' side holds a collection of the 'many'. Choose List, Set, or Map based on how you'll query — and encapsulate the collection behind meaningful methods.
